overview: NZME is New Zealand's largest multi-platform media company, publishing the NZ Herald and regional/community titles, operating a portfolio of radio brands (Newstalk ZB, ZM, Hauraki, The Hits, iHeartCountry) and digital audio via iHeartRadio, and owning the OneRoof residential property listings portal. Demerged from APN News & Media and dual-listed on the NZX and ASX in June 2016, NZME reports in NZD with a 31 December fiscal year end. The business is mid-transition from a legacy print/radio advertising model toward digital subscriptions, digital audio and property-listing revenue, against a backdrop of secular print decline, a slowly recovering but still-soft NZ advertising and housing market, and an unresolved, market-moving contest for board/company control by its largest shareholder.

business_model.summary: NZME earns revenue from three operating divisions -- Publishing, Audio and OneRoof -- through a mix of advertising (print, radio, digital display/programmatic), reader/subscriber revenue (print and digital-only news subscriptions), and property-listing/upgrade fees paid by real estate agents/vendors on OneRoof. Historically an advertising-led business, NZME has pursued a 'digital-first' and increasingly subscription-led strategy: digital subscriptions reached 250,000 by H1-2026 (70% digital-only), and management explicitly frames subscription and listings revenue as more stable and higher-quality than pure advertising income. GrabOne, a daily-deals e-commerce business, was divested in 2021 (sold for NZ$17.5m) and is no longer part of the group.

revenue_streams.name: Publishing (NZ Herald, BusinessDesk, regional/community print, digital subscriptions & advertising)
Audio (Newstalk ZB, ZM, Hauraki, The Hits, iHeartRadio, podcasting, iHeartCountry)
revenue_streams.trend: growing -- 15 consecutive months of YoY revenue growth through H1-2026, digital audio +16% YoY

revenue_streams.name: OneRoof (property listings, digital & print real estate)
revenue_streams.trend: mixed -- digital revenue growth has slowed sharply (+4% H1-2026 vs +19% FY2025) on a weak Auckland housing market, while print declines further

business_model.customer_type: Mixed B2C (news/audio subscribers and listeners) and B2B (advertisers, media agencies, and real estate agents/vendors on OneRoof)
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand -- no meaningful international revenue exposure
business_model.revenue_quality_notes: H1-2026 operating revenue was $167.0m (+1% YoY), with advertising revenue +2% (Audio the driver, up 8%) partly offset by a 3% decline in reader revenue (print subscriber volumes down 9%, offset only partially by 5% yield gains and 1% digital subscription revenue growth). Operating EBITDA grew 11% to $26.5m on a mix of modest revenue growth and continued cost discipline (opex down 1%). OneRoof underperformed expectations: digital revenue grew only 4% (well below plan) due to a slower Auckland market with longer selling times and cautious vendors, though EBITDA still grew 9% via cost control and a 15% decline in print revenue drag.

main_competitors: Stuff (NZ's other major newspaper/digital publisher, owned by Sinead Boucher; also a print-plant supplier/counterparty and periodic M&A counterparty to NZME)
Trade Me (NZ's dominant online marketplace, including Trade Me Property -- the clear #1 property portal, named 2026 Brand of the Year off record revenue and audience)
MediaWorks (competing radio group -- MoreFM, The Edge, George FM etc.)
Warner Bros. Discovery / Sky NZ / TVNZ (broadcast and streaming video, competing for advertising dollars)
Google and Meta (dominant recipients of NZ digital advertising spend; also a competitive/complementary counterparty via commercial news-licensing and content-supply deals)
realestate.co.nz (industry-owned property listing site) and homes.co.nz (owned by Trade Me since 2021)
competitive_position.market_position: Clear #1 in New Zealand news publishing (NZ Herald, the leading news app by launches) and #1 in commercial radio, with 15 consecutive months of YoY audio revenue growth to H1-2026 and market share gains against a shrinking radio ad pool. In property listings, OneRoof remains a distant #2 to Trade Me Property, which won 2026 Brand of the Year on record revenue and audience; OneRoof's growth has stalled in 2026 (digital revenue +4% H1-2026 vs +19% in FY2025) as the Auckland market weakens, even as the company reinvests in a new app, in-housed engineering and new leadership.

moat_factors.description: NZ Herald and Newstalk ZB are the most recognised news brands in the country, reaching roughly 9 in 10 Kiwis across NZME's platforms combined, supporting advertiser reach and subscriber trust; the NZ Herald app now has more launches than its nearest competitor.

Newstalk ZB and ZM/The Hits are top-rating shows nationally; audio revenue has grown faster than the market for 15 straight months, and agency-managed customer share of audio revenue has risen to 51% (from 43-46%), reflecting real commercial momentum and negotiating leverage.
NZME can bundle audio, publishing and OneRoof inventory for advertisers/agents in a way single-platform competitors cannot.

Property portals are classic winner-take-most two-sided markets; Trade Me's larger buyer audience and stronger 2026 brand momentum make it the default listing choice for agents, and OneRoof's #2 position -- even with a new app and in-housed technology -- has not closed the gap, with 2026 digital growth actually decelerating sharply.

moat_factors.factor: Regulatory/scale barriers to entry in radio and news
moat_factors.description: Broadcasting spectrum (AM/FM renewals for 2031 currently underway), existing newsroom infrastructure and journalist/on-air talent create real barriers for new entrants; the Commerce Commission's 2017-18 blocking of the NZME/Fairfax merger is evidence regulators view NZ media concentration as a serious competition issue.

weaknesses: Distant #2 (or weaker) in property listings against an entrenched, currently stronger-performing Trade Me Property, in a category with strong winner-take-most economics -- and OneRoof's 2026 growth has stalled

Legacy print cost base (presses, distribution, paper) remains a drag on margins even as print revenue shrinks; a new print plant (up to $15m investment, operational 2027) is required just to right-size capacity
Heavily dependent on the small, cyclical NZ advertising and housing markets with no geographic diversification
Structurally exposed to Google/Meta's share of digital ad spend; NZME's five-year Google content-supply agreement expires December 2026 and renewal/replacement terms are not yet settled
Small-cap scale (~NZ$150-250m market cap) limits capital available for reinvestment relative to global platform competitors

Unresolved, market-relevant shareholder/governance overhang: largest shareholder Jim Grenon has built a stake just under the 20% compulsory-takeover threshold under NZ law, creating persistent uncertainty about board control and strategic direction

growth_drivers: Audio momentum: 15 consecutive months of YoY revenue growth into H1-2026, digital audio +16% YoY, a new 10-year iHeartRadio commitment, iHeartCountry scaling to 21 frequencies nationwide, and 2026 General Election coverage expected to lift H2 news engagement

Digital subscriptions in Publishing: total subscriptions +6% YoY to 250,000 (70% now digital-only, +13pts YoY), a new NZ Herald app launched June 2026 (more launches than its nearest competitor, 57% of interactions now in-app), Herald NOW video (+132% video views YoY) and a dynamic paywall investment aimed at improving conversion and yield

OneRoof reinvestment: new app (+54% monthly active users since launch), in-housed technology/engineering team, new senior leadership, and headroom in upgrade penetration (33% national vs a 60%/40% Auckland/Rest-of-NZ ambition) provide a path back to growth once the Auckland housing market normalises

Cost-out programs: $12m of annualised savings fully realised through 2025/2026; a NEW round targeting $4m of annualised savings from Q4 2026 (full benefit in 2027) plus a further $3m in H1 2027 (full benefit 2028) via AI-enabled productivity/automation; a new, more efficient print plant (up to $15m capex, operational 2027, ~$7m annual savings by 2030); and improved Central Auckland lease terms (Heads of Terms agreed, pending final approval) lowering the fixed cost base

Cyclical recovery optionality: management explicitly guided FY2026 Operating EBITDA to be 'ahead of the 2025 result' and expects recovery momentum to improve into 2027, which would flow disproportionately to earnings given the operating leverage already demonstrated (11% EBITDA growth on 1% revenue growth in H1-2026)

AI/content monetisation: the five-year Google content-supply agreement expiring December 2026 is being actively renegotiated, with management explicitly targeting expanded content licensing and AI monetisation opportunities across global digital platforms as part of that renewal -- a potential new, largely incremental revenue stream

Consolidation optionality: prior (paused) discussions with Stuff around masthead/print-plant assets illustrate a recurring structural opportunity to reduce industry duplicate cost bases, though the most recent concrete outcome was the smaller Petone print-equipment purchase rather than a broader combination

business.description: Print subscriber volumes fell 9% YoY in H1-2026 and print advertising continues to shrink; digital growth (subscriptions +6%, digital publishing EBITDA +11%) is helping offset this at the EBITDA line but total reader revenue still declined 3% YoY.

business.risk: OneRoof competitive position and 2026 growth stall
business.description: OneRoof remains a clear #2 to a resurgent Trade Me Property (2026 Brand of the Year); OneRoof's digital revenue growth decelerated sharply to +4% in H1-2026 (from +19% in FY2025), driven by a weak, slow-to-sell Auckland market, raising the risk that the 'option value' thesis behind the 2025 strategic review takes longer to realise than hoped.

Largest shareholder Jim Grenon has increased his stake to just under 20% (the NZ compulsory-takeover trigger), continuing a pattern of aggressive on-market buying and prior board-composition activism; this creates an unresolved overhang on strategy, capital allocation and management stability, and could resurface as a fresh governance contest or a full takeover approach at any time.

business.risk: Advertiser/vendor dependence on a small, single-country market
business.description: 100% NZ revenue base with no geographic diversification; NZME's fortunes are tied entirely to NZ business, consumer and housing-market confidence.

NZME's five-year Google content-supply deal concludes December 2026; management says it is 'actively working to renew or replace it' but renewal terms, and thus a meaningful slice of digital/commercial revenue, are not yet locked in.

financial.description: Net debt was $19.4m at H1-2026 (down $13.9m YoY from $33.3m), leverage of 0.4x EBITDA, comfortably below the 0.5-1.0x target range -- balance sheet is currently conservative and interest cover is very strong (26.1x).

financial.risk: Dividend sustainability vs capex and investment needs
financial.description: Dividend policy targets 50-80% of free cash flow within the leverage band; a 3cps fully imputed interim dividend was declared for H1-2026 (payable 23 Sep 2026), consistent with the prior year. New capex commitments (up to $15m print plant through 2027, OneRoof/technology investment) will need to be funded alongside continued dividends, though BAU capex guidance of $10-12m for FY2026 remains modest.

NZME has repeatedly taken large non-cash goodwill/masthead impairments (e.g., $24.0m in FY2024), driving statutory NPAT to a loss in some years even when underlying cash generation was positive. H1-2026 statutory NPAT of $6.6m (vs a $0.4m loss in H1-2025) benefited from the absence of non-recurring costs; investors should focus on Operating EBITDA, Operating NPAT and free cash flow as the more representative measures, while recognising further impairments remain possible given still-depressed legacy print/masthead asset values.

regulatory.description: Under NZ takeovers law, a shareholder cannot increase a holding beyond 20% without triggering a full takeover offer; Jim Grenon's stake sitting just under that threshold (after a pattern of continued on-market buying) means a full takeover approach, a further governance contest, or continued creeping influence are all live possibilities that could materially affect strategy and the share price with little notice.

regulatory.risk: Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill in limbo
regulatory.description: The Bill, which would have required Google/Meta to negotiate payment for NZ news content, remains on hold by the Government (paused December 2024) with no confirmed revival. If never passed, NZME forgoes a potential incremental, mandated revenue stream and instead must rely on voluntary commercial negotiation (as with the expiring Google content-supply deal).

The Commerce Commission's 2017-18 rejection (upheld on appeal) of the NZME/Fairfax merger establishes a clear precedent that any large-scale NZME/Stuff combination would face serious competition-law scrutiny, constraining the most obvious industry-consolidation path.

macro.description: Management describes an environment where inflation remains high (4.1%), unemployment has risen to 5.6% (+0.4pts YoY), and the OCR saw its first increase in three years in mid-2026, signalling the end of the easing cycle; NZME expects the trading environment to 'remain volatile' through H2-2026 with only modest recovery, pushing a fuller recovery out to 2027.

OneRoof's revenue is directly levered to national residential listing/sale volumes; the Auckland market specifically is described as slow, with properties taking longer to sell and vendors cautious, directly capping OneRoof's 2026 growth regardless of product execution.

NZ mortgage rates and RBNZ policy directly influence both housing transaction volumes (OneRoof) and broader consumer/business confidence (advertising); the first OCR increase in three years (mid-2026) is a fresh headwind versus the earlier expected easing cycle.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: New Zealand traditional media advertising continues to shrink structurally as spend migrates to Google/Meta and digital-native channels; audio (radio + digital audio/podcasting) has proven the most resilient of NZME's segments, with total agency market ad spend up 2.0% in H1-2026 led by Digital (+4%), Outdoor (+7%) and Radio (+9%). Property/classifieds remains consolidated around a dominant Trade Me Property and a distant OneRoof. NZME's own commentary describes a 'volatile' trading environment through H2-2026 with recovery momentum expected to build into 2027.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High -- advertising and property-listing revenue are both classic late-cycle discretionary spend categories; NZME's earnings swing materially with the NZ economic and housing cycle, though cost discipline has recently allowed EBITDA to grow faster than revenue.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high indirect sensitivity via mortgage rates/housing turnover (OneRoof) and business/consumer confidence (advertising); low direct sensitivity given modest net debt ($19.4m) and very strong interest cover (26.1x). The first OCR increase in three years (mid-2026) is a fresh headwind to the previously assumed easing-cycle tailwind.
key_input_costs: Technology/digital platform development and AI tooling

recent_developments.event: FY2025 full-year results: operating revenue $345.1m (-1% YoY, +1% like-for-like), Operating EBITDA $62.3m (+15% YoY), Operating NPAT $17.7m, statutory NPAT $13.1m (vs $16.0m loss in FY2024), free cash flow $25.4m, net debt down to $15.5m. Total FY2025 dividends of 9.0cps declared, flat vs FY2024 (67% payout ratio). New CFO Jo Hempstead (ex-Warehouse Group) joined.
Kate Parsons appointed to the NZME board, continuing the board renewal that followed the 2025 Grenon-driven governance contest.

NZME's 2026 AGM confirmed the post-2025 board composition (Chairman Steven Joyce, directors including Jim Grenon and Bowen Pan, who chairs the OneRoof Advisory Board); management reiterated the OneRoof strategic review had identified a significant value-creation opportunity, with near-term focus on organic growth.

Chairman Steven Joyce made further on-market purchases of NZME shares (now holding just over 100,000 shares), while largest shareholder Jim Grenon continued accumulating stock through 2026, most recently spending roughly $2m to lift his holding to just under 20% -- the threshold beyond which a compulsory takeover offer is triggered under NZ law. This remains a live, unresolved governance/ownership overhang.

H1-2026 (six months to 30 June 2026) results: operating revenue $167.0m (+1% YoY), Operating EBITDA $26.5m (+11% YoY), Operating NPAT $6.6m (+100% YoY, EPS 3.5cps), statutory NPAT swung to a $6.6m profit (from a $0.4m loss in H1-2025), free cash flow $7.3m (+$5.1m YoY), net debt reduced to $19.4m (leverage 0.4x EBITDA, well within the 0.5-1.0x target). A fully imputed interim dividend of 3cps was declared, payable 23 September 2026, consistent with the prior year.

Divisional detail: Audio delivered its 15th consecutive month of YoY revenue growth (+8%, EBITDA +19%); Digital Publishing EBITDA grew 11% (subscriptions +6% to 250,000, 70% digital-only) offsetting print declines; OneRoof revenue growth stalled well below expectations (digital revenue +4% vs +19% in FY2025) due to a slow Auckland market, though EBITDA still grew 9% on cost discipline.

New cost-out program announced: $4m of annualised savings targeted from Q4 2026 (full benefit 2027) plus a further $3m in H1 2027 (full benefit 2028), leveraging AI-driven productivity and automation, alongside a new, more efficient print plant (up to $15m capex through 2027, breakeven ~2030, ~$7m annual savings thereafter) and improved Central Auckland lease terms (Heads of Terms agreed, pending final landlord/shareholder approval, backdated to November 2025).

Management guided FY2026 Operating EBITDA to be 'ahead of the 2025 result' (subject to no material deterioration in H2 trading conditions), and disclosed that the five-year Google content-supply agreement concludes December 2026, with NZME 'actively working to renew or replace it while expanding content licensing and AI monetisation opportunities across global digital platforms.'

OneRoof new app update: monthly active users up 54% since launch in March 2026, daily active users up 53%, users viewing listings daily up 24%; management flagged 'market recovery still ahead' for Auckland and headroom in national upgrade-product penetration (33% national vs a 60%/40% Auckland/Rest-of-NZ ambition) as the key medium-term OneRoof growth levers.

items.vs_prior: raised / new formal guidance (FY2025 result gave no formal FY2026 EBITDA number)
items.notes: Explicitly caveated: 'subject to trading conditions in the second half, and assuming no material deterioration in market conditions.' Follows an 11% EBITDA increase in H1-2026 and management's expectation that recovery momentum improves further into 2027.
Excludes the separate, incremental up-to-$15m print plant investment (~$7m expected in 2026, ~$8m in 2027).

items.target: New program: $4m annualised savings from Q4 2026 (full benefit 2027); further $3m annualised from H1 2027 (full benefit 2028)
items.vs_prior: new, incremental to the prior $12m program completed in 2025
items.notes: Delivered via AI-enabled productivity/automation initiatives; management says 'further opportunities expected to support revenue growth' beyond pure cost reduction.

items.target: Up to $15m total investment (~$7m in 2026, ~$8m in 2027); ~$3-5m savings from 2028, ~$7m annualised savings from 2029, investment breakeven ~2030
items.notes: 3-year payback upon becoming operational (new plant operational 2027, old plant decommissioned).

items.target: 50-80% of free cash flow, subject to remaining within 0.5-1.0x EBITDA target leverage
items.notes: H1-2026 interim dividend of 3cps declared (fully imputed), payable 23 September 2026, flat vs the prior-year interim; FY2025 final dividend of 6cps was paid in March 2026.

items.target: No formal separation/monetisation decision; near-term priority is organic growth via new app, in-housed technology, and new leadership
items.notes: Management continues to describe a 'significant value creation opportunity' but 2026 execution has been slower than FY2025's momentum, given the weak Auckland housing market.

items.target: Renew or replace prior to December 2026 expiry, while expanding content licensing/AI monetisation opportunities
items.notes: No confirmed terms yet; a swing factor for both digital advertising/other revenue and AI-related monetisation optionality.

guidance.management_commentary: Management said the first six months of 2026 focused on 'returning to revenue growth while at the same time maintaining tight cost discipline,' and expects the trading environment to 'remain volatile' in H2-2026 as consumer confidence stays soft and discretionary spending is restrained by higher living costs and mortgage rates, with 'recovery momentum to improve into 2027.' The company reiterated it is 'well positioned to continue to deliver strong dividend returns while also prioritising selective investment in growth and cost out opportunities,' with near-term investment prioritised behind OneRoof, digital subscriptions and video.

bull_case: Audio is now a genuine growth engine, not just a defensive legacy asset -- 15 consecutive months of YoY revenue growth, digital audio +16% YoY, rising agency share, and a new 10-year iHeartRadio commitment support continued outperformance versus a soft broader ad market

Demonstrated operating leverage and cost discipline: H1-2026 EBITDA grew 11% on just 1% revenue growth, management has explicitly guided FY2026 EBITDA ahead of FY2025, and a new $4m+$3m cost-out program plus a more efficient print plant and improved Auckland lease terms should structurally lower the cost base into 2027-2030

Balance sheet is conservative and improving (net debt down to $19.4m, leverage 0.4x, interest cover 26.1x), funding both a continued dividend (running yield reported around 8%+ on some analyses) and selective growth capex without stress

OneRoof retains real optionality despite a soft 2026: the new app has driven +54% monthly active user growth, technology has been brought in-house for faster iteration, and national upgrade-penetration headroom (33% vs a 60%/40% target) offers a credible growth path once the Auckland housing cycle turns

Cyclical trough dynamics remain in place: NZ business/consumer confidence and housing activity are still below normal levels per management's own data, so a genuine 2027 recovery would flow disproportionately to earnings given the leverage already demonstrated in 2025-2026's cost-out execution
bear_case: The Jim Grenon shareholding/governance overhang is unresolved and now more acute: his stake sits just under the 20% compulsory-takeover trigger after a pattern of continued aggressive buying, creating persistent uncertainty about strategic direction, board stability, and the potential for a full takeover approach or renewed governance conflict with little warning

OneRoof's 2026 momentum has stalled sharply (digital revenue +4% vs +19% in FY2025) against a resurgent, 2026-Brand-of-the-Year Trade Me Property -- the competitive gap in property listings, a classic winner-take-most category, is not closing and may be widening

Print decline continues to erode the reader-revenue base (print subscriber volumes -9% YoY in H1-2026) even as digital subscription growth only partially offsets it, and total reader revenue fell 3% YoY -- the print cost base requires fresh capital (up to $15m for a new plant) simply to remain viable

The five-year Google content-supply agreement expires December 2026 with renewal terms not yet locked in, creating near-term revenue/monetisation uncertainty precisely as management is counting on this relationship for incremental AI-licensing upside

A softening macro backdrop -- inflation still at 4.1%, unemployment rising to 5.6%, and the first OCR increase in three years in mid-2026 -- pushes NZME's own expected recovery out to 2027, meaning near-term earnings remain hostage to a small, single-country, structurally-challenged advertising and housing market with no geographic diversification to cushion a renewed downturn
